reminder: A strong orientation gives each edge of a [graph](c:graph) a direction so that every vertex can reach every other vertex.
definition: An orientation of an undirected [graph](c:graph) $G$ gives each [edge](c:edge) $uv$ exactly one direction, either $u\to v$ or $v\to u$. The orientation is strong when the resulting [directed graph](c:directed-graph) is strongly connected: for all vertices $u$ and $v$ there is a directed [path](c:path) from $u$ to $v$.
examples: Orient the cycle $C_n$ around the cycle, so that each edge points to the next vertex; this orientation is strong.
Every [2-edge-connected graph](c:2-edge-connected-graph) has a strong orientation (Robbins' theorem), for example the complete graph $K_4$.
Non-example: the path with vertices $1,2,3$ and edges $12$ and $23$ has no strong orientation, because after edge $12$ is oriented one way, no directed path leads back.

reminder: A strongly continuous semigroup is a family of bounded operators $T(t)$ with $T(s+t)=T(s)T(t)$ and continuous orbits $t\mapsto T(t)x$.
definition: A strongly continuous [semigroup](c:semigroup) on a [Banach space](c:banach-space) $X$ is a family $(T(t))_{t\ge0}$ of [bounded operators](c:bounded-linear-operator) with $T(0)=I$ and $T(s+t)=T(s)T(t)$ for all $s,t\ge0$, such that $t\mapsto T(t)x$ is [continuous](c:continuous-function) from $[0,\infty)$ to $X$ for every $x\in X$. Equivalently, $T(t)x\to x$ as $t\to0^+$ for every $x\in X$.
examples: For a bounded operator $A$, the family $T(t)=e^{tA}$ is a strongly continuous semigroup.
On $L^2(\mathbb{R})$ the translation family $(T(t)f)(x)=f(x+t)$ is a strongly continuous semigroup.
Non-example: the same translation family on $L^\infty(\mathbb{R})$ is not strongly continuous, because for $f=\mathbf 1_{[0,\infty)}$ the norm $\|T(t)f-f\|_\infty$ equals $1$ for every $t>0$.

steps: Take the bounded operators on $X$ with composition as the product.
Composition is associative and has the identity $I$, so these operators form a [semigroup](c:semigroup).
The law $T(s+t)=T(s)T(t)$ makes $\{T(t)\}$ a commutative sub-semigroup, indexed by the times $t\ge0$.
The strongly continuous case adds that every orbit $t\mapsto T(t)x$ is continuous.
links.why: It shows that the algebra of time evolution is the semigroup law, and that continuity is the extra analytic condition.

reminder: A Sturm-Liouville problem asks for numbers $\lambda$ and nonzero functions $y$ with $-(py')'+qy=\lambda wy$ and given boundary conditions.
definition: A Sturm-Liouville problem on an [interval](c:interval) $[a,b]$ is the second-order linear [ordinary differential equation](c:ordinary-differential-equation) $-(py')'+qy=\lambda wy$, with $p,w>0$ and $p',q,w$ continuous, together with separated boundary conditions $\alpha y(a)+\beta y'(a)=0$ and $\gamma y(b)+\delta y'(b)=0$. A solution is an [eigenvalue](c:eigenvalue) $\lambda$ with a nonzero eigenfunction $y$ that satisfies the equation and both conditions.
examples: The problem $-y''=\lambda y$ on $[0,\pi]$ with $y(0)=y(\pi)=0$ has eigenvalues $\lambda_n=n^2$ and eigenfunctions $\sin nx$ for $n=1,2,\dots$.
The problem $-y''=\lambda y$ on $[0,1]$ with $y'(0)=y'(1)=0$ has eigenvalues $\lambda_n=n^2\pi^2$ and eigenfunctions $\cos n\pi x$ for $n=0,1,2,\dots$.
Non-example: $y'''=\lambda y$ with boundary conditions is not a Sturm-Liouville problem, because its equation has order three, not two.

reminder: A substructure is a subset of a structure that contains the constants, is closed under the functions, and carries the restricted relations.
definition: Let $M$ be a [structure](c:structure) for a language $L$ of [first-order logic](c:first-order-logic). A substructure $N\subseteq M$ is a [subset](c:subset) that contains the value of every constant symbol, is closed under every function symbol of $L$, and carries the restrictions of the functions and relations of $M$. Then $N$ is itself an $L$-structure, and the inclusion $N\to M$ preserves all atomic formulas.
examples: In the language $\{+,0\}$, the structure $(\mathbb{N},+,0)$ is a substructure of $(\mathbb{Z},+,0)$.
In the language $\{<\}$, which has only a relation symbol, every subset of $(\mathbb{R},<)$ is a substructure, for example $(\mathbb{Q},<)$.
Non-example: in the language $\{+,0\}$, the set $\{1,2,3\}\subseteq\mathbb{Z}$ is not a substructure of $(\mathbb{Z},+,0)$, because it misses $0$ and it is not closed under $+$ (as $2+3=5$).

steps: Start with a substructure $N\subseteq M$.
Closure under the functions makes every atomic formula with parameters in $N$ true in $N$ exactly when it is true in $M$.
The elementary case adds the same equivalence for every first-order formula, including formulas with quantifiers.
Then $N$ is an [elementary substructure](c:elementary-substructure) of $M$.
links.why: It shows what an elementary substructure adds to a substructure: agreement on all formulas, not only on atomic ones.

steps: Take the language of groups, with symbols for the product, the inverse and the identity.
A substructure of a group in this language contains the identity and is closed under product and inverse.
These are exactly the conditions for a [subgroup](c:subgroup).
So the substructures of a group, in this language, are its subgroups.
links.why: It shows that subgroups, subrings and similar sub-objects are substructures for a suitable language.

reminder: A summability method assigns a generalized limit to some sequences by a linear rule, often by averaging with a matrix.
definition: A summability method is a linear rule that assigns a number to some [sequences](c:sequence) of numbers, usually given by an infinite [matrix](c:matrix) $A=(a_{nk})$: the sequence $(s_k)$ is $A$-summable to $L$ when $(As)_n=\sum_k a_{nk}s_k$ converges for every $n$ and $(As)_n\to L$ as $n\to\infty$. The method is regular when every convergent sequence is summable to its ordinary [limit](c:limit-of-a-sequence).
examples: The Cesàro method has $a_{nk}=1/n$ for $1\le k\le n$ and $0$ otherwise; it averages the first $n$ terms, so $0,1,0,1,\dots$ is summable to $1/2$.
The identity matrix $A=I$ gives the ordinary limit of a sequence.

Non-example: the rule $s\mapsto\limsup s_n$ is not a summability method, because it is not linear: $(1,0,1,0,\dots)$ and $(0,1,0,1,\dots)$ both have $\limsup 1$, but their sum $(1,1,1,\dots)$ has $\limsup 1$, not $2$.

steps: Take the identity matrix $A=I$, so $(As)_n=s_n$.
Then $s$ is $I$-summable to $L$ exactly when $s_n\to L$.
So ordinary convergence is the summability method of the identity matrix.
A general summability method may also sum sequences that do not converge.
links.why: It shows that a summability method extends the idea of a limit to more sequences.

steps: Start with a [regular summation method](c:regular-summation-method) $A$.
By definition it is a summability method.
Regularity adds that every convergent sequence $s_n\to L$ is $A$-summable to the same number $L$.
So the regular methods are the summability methods that extend ordinary convergence.
links.why: It shows that regularity is an extra condition, and that not every summability method has it.

reminder: A super vector space is a $\mathbb{Z}/2$-graded vector space whose swap map carries the sign $(-1)^{|v||w|}$.
definition: A super vector space is a [graded vector space](c:graded-vector-space) $V=V_0\oplus V_1$ with grading group $\mathbb{Z}/2$, where $V_0$ holds the even vectors and $V_1$ the odd vectors. The [tensor product](c:tensor-product) of super vector spaces has the [braiding](c:braiding) $v\otimes w\mapsto(-1)^{|v||w|}\,w\otimes v$ on homogeneous vectors, which makes super vector spaces a [symmetric monoidal category](c:symmetric-monoidal-category) over a [vector space](c:vector-space) base field.
examples: The space $\mathbb{R}^{p|q}=\mathbb{R}^p\oplus\mathbb{R}^q$ has $p$ even and $q$ odd basis vectors.
Every ordinary vector space is a super vector space with $V_1=0$.
The exterior algebra $\Lambda(\mathbb{R}^n)$ is a super vector space, with the even-degree and odd-degree parts as $V_0$ and $V_1$.
Non-example: a $\mathbb{Z}$-graded vector space is not a super vector space as it stands, because its grading group is $\mathbb{Z}$, not $\mathbb{Z}/2$; one must first reduce degrees mod $2$.

steps: Start with a [graded vector space](c:graded-vector-space) $V=\bigoplus_{g\in G}V_g$ for an abelian group $G$.
Take $G=\mathbb{Z}/2$, so that $V=V_0\oplus V_1$ has an even part and an odd part.
Replace the plain swap of tensor factors by the swap with the sign $(-1)^{|v||w|}$.
The result is a super vector space.
links.why: It shows that a super vector space is a graded vector space with a new symmetry, and that the sign rule is the new content.

reminder: A super vielbein is a frame of the tangent bundle of a supermanifold, with even and odd frame fields.
definition: On a [supermanifold](c:supermanifold) of dimension $d|N$, a super vielbein is a frame field of its [tangent bundle](c:tangent-bundle): $d$ even and $N$ odd vector fields that are linearly independent at every point. It is the supergeometric version of a [vielbein](c:vielbein); the dual coframe has $d$ even and $N$ odd one-forms.
examples: On $\mathbb{R}^{d|N}$ with coordinates $x^a$ and $\theta^\alpha$, the coordinate fields $\partial_{x^a}$ and $\partial_{\theta^\alpha}$ form a super vielbein.
Flat superspace has a frame of $d$ even and $N$ odd supertranslation-invariant vector fields, which serves as its flat super vielbein.
Non-example: on $\mathbb{R}^{1|1}$ the fields $x\,\partial_x$ and $\partial_\theta$ are not a super vielbein, because $x\,\partial_x$ vanishes at $x=0$, so the fields are not independent there.

steps: Take a supermanifold of dimension $d|0$, which is an ordinary $d$-dimensional manifold.
A frame field of its tangent bundle then has only even frame fields.
That frame field is a [vielbein](c:vielbein).
So the super vielbein adds the odd frame fields to the vielbein.
links.why: It shows that a vielbein is the purely even case of a super vielbein.

reminder: A surface integral adds up a function or a vector field over a surface, weighted by the area element.
definition: Let $S$ be a [surface](c:surface) with a parametrization $\mathbf r:D\to S$, where $D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2$. The surface [integral](c:integral) of a function $f$ is $\iint_S f\,dS=\iint_D f(\mathbf r(u,v))\,\lVert\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\rVert\,du\,dv$, using the [cross product](c:cross-product), and the flux of a [vector field](c:vector-field) $\mathbf F$ is $\iint_S\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n\,dS$ for a unit normal field $\mathbf n$ of an oriented surface.
examples: For the unit sphere $S$, $\iint_S 1\,dS=4\pi$, the area of the sphere.
The outward flux of $\mathbf F(x,y,z)=(x,y,z)$ through the unit sphere is $4\pi$, because $\mathbf F\cdot\mathbf n=1$ on the sphere.
Non-example: the flux of a vector field through a Möbius band is not defined, because the band has no continuous unit normal field.

steps: Parametrize the surface by $\mathbf r:D\to S$ with $D\subseteq\mathbb{R}^2$.
The area element $dS=\lVert\mathbf r_u\times\mathbf r_v\rVert\,du\,dv$ measures small pieces of $S$.
Summing $f\,dS$ over finer and finer pieces of $S$ gives the surface integral as a limit of sums.
So it is an [integral](c:integral) of $f$ whose domain is a surface instead of an interval.
links.why: It shows that a surface integral is an ordinary accumulated total, with the area element as the weight.

reminder: A syzygy of generators $m_1,\dots,m_n$ of a module is a relation $r_1m_1+\dots+r_nm_n=0$ among them.
definition: Let $R$ be a [ring](c:ring) and $N$ an $R$-[module](c:module) generated by $m_1,\dots,m_n$. A syzygy is a tuple $(r_1,\dots,r_n)\in R^n$ with $r_1m_1+\dots+r_nm_n=0$; the syzygies form the [kernel](c:kernel-of-a-homomorphism) of the map $R^n\to N$ that sends $e_i$ to $m_i$, a [submodule](c:submodule) of the [free module](c:free-module) $R^n$.
examples: For $N=\mathbb{Z}/6$ over $\mathbb{Z}$ with the generator $m_1=1$, the syzygies are the multiples $6k$.
For the ideal $(x,y)$ of $k[x,y]$ with generators $x,y$, the tuple $(y,-x)$ is a syzygy, because $yx-xy=0$, and it generates all syzygies.
Non-example: $(1,1)$ is not a syzygy of the generators $x,y$ of $(x,y)$, because $x+y\ne0$.

steps: Take generators $m_1,\dots,m_n$ of the module $N$ and the free module $R^n$ with basis $e_1,\dots,e_n$.
Define the homomorphism $\pi:R^n\to N$ by $\pi(e_i)=m_i$.
A tuple $(r_i)$ lies in the kernel of $\pi$ exactly when $\sum r_im_i=0$.
So the module of syzygies is the [kernel](c:kernel-of-a-homomorphism) of $\pi$.
links.why: It shows that syzygies are the kernel of a presentation map, so kernel facts give facts about syzygies.

reminder: In a $T_0$ space, any two different points are separated by an open set that contains exactly one of them.
definition: A [topological space](c:topological-space) $X$ is $T_0$ (a Kolmogorov space) when for all points $x\ne y$ there is an [open set](c:open-set) that contains one of them and not the other. Equivalently, distinct points have distinct closures.
examples: Every [Hausdorff space](c:hausdorff-space) is $T_0$, for example $\mathbb{R}$ with its usual topology.
The Sierpiński space $\{0,1\}$ with open sets $\emptyset,\{1\},\{0,1\}$ is $T_0$: the open set $\{1\}$ separates the two points.
Non-example: an indiscrete space with two points is not $T_0$, because its only open sets are $\emptyset$ and the whole space.

steps: Let $X$ be a [T1 space](c:t1-space) and let $x\ne y$ be points of $X$.
By $T_1$ there is an open set $U$ with $x\in U$ and $y\notin U$.
This $U$ contains one of the two points and not the other, so $X$ is $T_0$.
The $T_1$ case adds that such an open set exists in both directions.
links.why: It shows that $T_1$ is $T_0$ with separation in both directions, so every $T_1$ space satisfies $T_0$ results.

steps: Let $X$ be a [Hausdorff space](c:hausdorff-space) and let $x\ne y$ be points of $X$.
There are disjoint open sets $U\ni x$ and $V\ni y$.
Then $U$ contains $x$ and not $y$, because $U$ and $V$ are disjoint.
So $X$ is $T_0$; the Hausdorff case adds disjoint open sets around both points.
links.why: It shows that every Hausdorff space is $T_0$, so results for $T_0$ spaces apply to the spaces of analysis.

reminder: The tail sigma-algebra holds the events that do not depend on any finite set of the random variables $X_n$.
definition: For a [sequence](c:sequence) $X_1,X_2,\dots$ of [random variables](c:random-variable), let $\mathcal F_n=\sigma(X_n,X_{n+1},\dots)$ be the [sigma-algebra](c:sigma-algebra) generated by the variables from index $n$ on. The tail sigma-algebra is $\mathcal T=\bigcap_{n\ge1}\mathcal F_n$, and its elements are the tail events.
examples: The event that $\sum X_n$ converges is a tail event, because a change of finitely many terms does not change convergence.
The event $\{X_n\ge1\text{ for infinitely many }n\}$ is a tail event.

Non-example: for independent fair coin flips $X_n\in\{0,1\}$, the event $\{X_1=1\}$ is not a tail event, because it has probability $1/2$, while tail events of independent variables have probability $0$ or $1$.

steps: Each $\mathcal F_n$ is a [sigma-algebra](c:sigma-algebra) of events.
An intersection of sigma-algebras is again a sigma-algebra.
So $\mathcal T=\bigcap_n\mathcal F_n$ is a sigma-algebra, and it lies inside every $\mathcal F_n$.
links.why: It shows that probability and measure apply to tail events, as to the events of any sigma-algebra.

reminder: The tangent bundle of a manifold is the union of all its tangent spaces, and it is again a manifold.
definition: For a [smooth manifold](c:smooth-manifold) $M$, the tangent bundle is $TM=\bigsqcup_{p\in M}T_pM$, the disjoint union of all [tangent spaces](c:tangent-space), with the projection $\pi:TM\to M$ that sends $T_pM$ to $p$. A chart of $M$ gives a chart of $TM$ by the point and the components of the vector, so $TM$ is a manifold of dimension $2\dim M$ and a [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) of rank $\dim M$ over $M$.
examples: For $M=\mathbb{R}^n$ we have $T\mathbb{R}^n=\mathbb{R}^n\times\mathbb{R}^n$: a point and a vector at that point.
The tangent bundle of the circle is trivial, $TS^1\cong S^1\times\mathbb{R}$.
The tangent bundle of $S^2$ is not trivial, because by the hairy ball theorem every vector field on $S^2$ has a zero.
Non-example: a single tangent space $T_pM$ is not the tangent bundle, which contains the tangent spaces of all points of $M$.

steps: Let $M$ be a smooth $n$-manifold and form $TM$ with its projection $\pi:TM\to M$.
Every fibre $\pi^{-1}(p)=T_pM$ is an $n$-dimensional vector space.
A chart $U\to\mathbb{R}^n$ gives a local trivialization $\pi^{-1}(U)\cong U\times\mathbb{R}^n$ that is linear on fibres.
So $TM$ is a [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle) of rank $n$ over $M$.
links.why: It shows that results on vector bundles, such as sections and trivializations, apply to vector fields on a manifold.

reminder: A tangent segment joins a point outside a circle to the point where a tangent line from it touches the circle.
definition: Let $P$ be a point outside a [circle](c:circle) with center $O$ and radius $r$. A tangent segment from $P$ is a [line segment](c:line-segment) $PT$, where $T$ lies on the circle and the [line](c:line) $PT$ is tangent to the circle at $T$; its length is $\sqrt{OP^2-r^2}$. From each outside point there are exactly two tangent segments, and they have equal length.
examples: If $OP=5$ and $r=3$, both tangent segments from $P$ have length $4$.
In a quadrilateral with an inscribed circle, each vertex has two tangent segments to the circle, and they have equal length.
Non-example: the segment from $P$ to a point $Q$ of the circle on a secant line through $P$ is not a tangent segment, because that line meets the circle at a second point.

reminder: A tangential quadrilateral is a convex quadrilateral whose four sides all touch one circle inside it.
definition: A tangential quadrilateral is a convex [quadrilateral](c:quadrilateral) that has an [incircle](c:incircle): a [circle](c:circle) inside it that is tangent to all four sides. In every tangential quadrilateral with consecutive sides $a,b,c,d$, the sums of opposite sides are equal, $a+c=b+d$ (Pitot's theorem).
examples: Every square and every rhombus is tangential, with the incircle centered at the intersection of the diagonals.
Every convex kite is tangential.
Non-example: a rectangle with sides $1$ and $2$ is not tangential, because opposite sides sum to $2$ and $4$.

steps: Start with a convex [quadrilateral](c:quadrilateral).
Add the condition that some circle touches all four sides.
Then each vertex has two equal tangent segments, so the sums of opposite sides are equal.
The quadrilateral is then tangential.
links.why: It shows which condition a tangential quadrilateral adds to a general one, and why opposite sides then have equal sums.

steps: Let $ABCD$ be a [square](c:square) with side $s$.
The circle with the center of the square and radius $s/2$ touches all four sides.
So the square is a tangential quadrilateral.
links.why: It shows that squares, and with the same argument rhombi, are tangential quadrilaterals.

reminder: A neutral Tannakian category is an abelian tensor category with duals and an exact faithful tensor functor to vector spaces.
definition: A neutral Tannakian category over a [field](c:field) $k$ is a $k$-linear [abelian category](c:abelian-category) $\mathcal C$ with a [symmetric monoidal](c:symmetric-monoidal-category) structure, with duals for all objects and with $\mathrm{End}(\mathbf 1)=k$, that has a [fiber functor](c:fiber-functor): an exact faithful $k$-linear tensor functor $\omega:\mathcal C\to\mathrm{Vect}_k$. By Tannaka reconstruction, $\mathcal C$ is then equivalent to the category of finite-dimensional [representations](c:group-representation) of the affine group scheme $\mathrm{Aut}^\otimes(\omega)$.
examples: The category of finite-dimensional vector spaces over $k$ is Tannakian, with the identity functor as fiber functor.
For a group $G$, the finite-dimensional representations of $G$ over $k$ form a Tannakian category, with the forgetful functor as fiber functor.

Non-example: over a field of characteristic $0$, the finite-dimensional super vector spaces with the sign braiding are not Tannakian, because the odd line has dimension $-1$, while a fiber functor gives dimensions that are non-negative integers.

steps: Start with a Tannakian category $\mathcal C$ over $k$.
By definition it has a symmetric tensor product $\otimes$ with a unit object $\mathbf 1$.
So $\mathcal C$ is a [symmetric monoidal category](c:symmetric-monoidal-category).
The Tannakian case adds an abelian structure, duals and a fiber functor.
links.why: It shows which conditions turn a symmetric monoidal category into a category of representations.

reminder: The Tate module of an abelian group $A$ at a prime $p$ is the inverse limit of the subgroups $A[p^n]$.
definition: Let $A$ be an [abelian group](c:abelian-group) and $p$ a [prime number](c:prime-number). The Tate module is $T_p(A)=\varprojlim_n A[p^n]$, the inverse [limit](c:limit-category-theory) of the [torsion](c:p-torsion) subgroups $A[p^n]=\{a\in A:p^na=0\}$ along the maps $A[p^{n+1}]\to A[p^n]$, $a\mapsto pa$. It is a module over the [$p$-adic integers](c:p-adic-integer).
examples: For the [Prüfer group](c:prufer-group) $\mathbb{Z}[1/p]/\mathbb{Z}$, the subgroup $A[p^n]$ is $\mathbb{Z}/p^n$ and $T_p(A)\cong\mathbb{Z}_p$.
For an [elliptic curve](c:elliptic-curve) $E$ over an algebraically closed field of characteristic not $p$, $T_p(E)\cong\mathbb{Z}_p^2$.
Non-example: the $p$-torsion subgroup $A[p]$ alone is not the Tate module; it is only the first term of the inverse system.

steps: Form the diagram $\cdots\to A[p^3]\to A[p^2]\to A[p]$ of abelian groups, with the maps $a\mapsto pa$.
Its [limit](c:limit-category-theory) is the group of compatible sequences $(a_n)$ with $a_n\in A[p^n]$ and $pa_{n+1}=a_n$.
This limit is the Tate module $T_p(A)$.
So the Tate module is the limit of one fixed diagram of torsion subgroups.
links.why: It shows that properties of limits, such as exactness conditions, apply to Tate modules.

reminder: Telescopic localization at height $n$ is the Bousfield localization of spectra at the telescope of a finite spectrum with a $v_n$-self map.
definition: Fix a [prime](c:prime-number) $p$ and $n\ge0$. Let $X$ be a type $n$ [finite spectrum](c:finite-spectrum) that is [$p$-local](c:p-local-spectrum), with a $v_n$-self map $v:\Sigma^dX\to X$, and let $T(n)$ be the telescope, the [homotopy colimit](c:homotopy-colimit) of $X\to\Sigma^{-d}X\to\Sigma^{-2d}X\to\cdots$. Telescopic localization at height $n$ is the [Bousfield localization of spectra](c:bousfield-localization-of-spectra) at $T(n)$.
examples: At height $0$ the telescope is the rational sphere spectrum, and the localization is rationalization.
At height $1$ the telescopic localization agrees with the localization at the [Morava K-theory](c:morava-k-theory) $K(1)$.
Non-example: for $n\ge2$ the localization at $K(n)$ is not the telescopic localization, because $T(n)$ and $K(n)$ differ in Bousfield class there (the telescope conjecture fails).

steps: Take the telescope $T(n)$ as the spectrum that defines the homology theory $E$.
Call a map $f$ of spectra a $T(n)$-equivalence when $T(n)\wedge f$ is an equivalence.
The [Bousfield localization of spectra](c:bousfield-localization-of-spectra) at $T(n)$ inverts all $T(n)$-equivalences.
This localization is the telescopic localization at height $n$.
links.why: It shows that telescopic localization is the Bousfield localization at one chosen family of spectra, so general localization results apply.

reminder: A tempered distribution is a continuous linear functional on the Schwartz space of rapidly decreasing smooth functions.
definition: A tempered distribution on [Euclidean space](c:euclidean-space) $\mathbb{R}^n$ is a linear map $u:\mathcal S(\mathbb{R}^n)\to\mathbb{C}$ on the [Schwartz space](c:schwartz-space) that is continuous: for some $C$ and $N$, $|u(\varphi)|\le C\sup_{|\alpha|,|\beta|\le N}\sup_x|x^\alpha\partial^\beta\varphi(x)|$ for all $\varphi$. It is a [distribution](c:distribution) of at most polynomial growth, and its Fourier transform is again defined.
examples: Every measurable function $f$ of polynomial growth gives the tempered distribution $u_f(\varphi)=\int f\varphi\,dx$, for example $f=1$ or $f=x^2$.
The Dirac delta $\delta(\varphi)=\varphi(0)$ and all its derivatives are tempered distributions.
Non-example: the function $e^{x^2}$ defines a distribution on $\mathbb{R}$ but not a tempered one, because $\int e^{x^2}\varphi\,dx$ diverges for $\varphi(x)=e^{-x^2/2}$.

steps: Let $u$ be a tempered distribution, a continuous linear map on $\mathcal S$.
The test functions $C_c^\infty$ lie inside $\mathcal S$, and the inclusion is continuous.
So the restriction of $u$ to $C_c^\infty$ is a [distribution](c:distribution).
Nothing is lost, because $C_c^\infty$ is dense in $\mathcal S$; the tempered case adds the growth bound.
links.why: It shows that a tempered distribution is a distribution with a growth bound, which is what makes the Fourier transform possible.

reminder: A term is an expression of a formal language, built from variables and function symbols, that stands for an element.
definition: In a formal language, a term is an expression that denotes an element. Every [variable](c:variable) and every constant symbol is a term, and if $f$ is an $n$-ary function symbol and $t_1,\dots,t_n$ are terms, then $f(t_1,\dots,t_n)$ is a term. In [type](c:type) theory, a term $z:Z$ is an expression of type $Z$; in sets it is an [element](c:element) $z\in Z$.
examples: In the language of rings, $x\cdot(y+1)$ and $0$ are terms.
In arithmetic, $S(S(0))+x$ is a term; it stands for the number $2+x$.
Non-example: $x+y=0$ is not a term but a formula, because it states a fact instead of denoting an element.

steps: Let $x$ be a [variable](c:variable) of the language.
By the first rule of the definition, $x$ is a term.
So every variable is a term, and general terms add the application of function symbols.
links.why: It shows that variables are the simplest terms, and that all other terms are built from them.

reminder: A theta function is a holomorphic section of a polarizing line bundle on a complex torus.
definition: Let $T=\mathbb{C}^g/\Lambda$ be a [complex torus](c:complex-torus) with a [line bundle](c:line-bundle) $L$ that gives a principal polarization. A theta function is a global section of $L$ that is a [holomorphic function](c:holomorphic-function) in the local trivializations; on $\mathbb{C}^g$ it is a holomorphic $\theta$ with $\theta(z+\lambda)=e_\lambda(z)\theta(z)$ for all $\lambda\in\Lambda$, where $e_\lambda$ is a fixed nowhere-zero factor.
examples: The Jacobi theta function $\theta(z,\tau)=\sum_{n\in\mathbb{Z}}e^{\pi in^2\tau+2\pi inz}$ with $\operatorname{Im}\tau>0$ satisfies $\theta(z+1)=\theta(z)$ and $\theta(z+\tau)=e^{-\pi i\tau-2\pi iz}\theta(z)$.

The Riemann theta function $\theta(z,\Omega)=\sum_{m\in\mathbb{Z}^g}e^{\pi im^{T}\Omega m+2\pi im^{T}z}$, for $\Omega$ symmetric with positive definite imaginary part, is a theta function on $\mathbb{C}^g/(\mathbb{Z}^g+\Omega\mathbb{Z}^g)$.
Non-example: the Weierstrass function $\wp$ is not a theta function, because it is meromorphic with a double pole at the lattice points, not holomorphic.

steps: Take $g=1$ and the elliptic curve $\mathbb{C}/(\mathbb{Z}+\tau\mathbb{Z})$ with $\operatorname{Im}\tau>0$.
A line bundle of degree one on it gives a principal polarization.
Its space of holomorphic sections has dimension one, spanned by Jacobi's $\theta(z,\tau)$ up to a shift of $z$.
So the [Jacobi theta function](c:jacobi-theta-function) is the one-dimensional theta function.
links.why: It shows that Jacobi's function is the genus one case of the general theta function.

steps: Take $\Omega$ symmetric with positive definite imaginary part, and the torus $\mathbb{C}^g/(\mathbb{Z}^g+\Omega\mathbb{Z}^g)$.
The series $\theta(z,\Omega)$ converges to a holomorphic function with a fixed factor for each lattice translation.
So it is a section of a principally polarizing line bundle.
Hence the [Riemann theta function](c:riemann-theta-function) is a theta function.
links.why: It shows that the Riemann theta function is the standard explicit theta function of a principally polarized torus.

reminder: The time-ordered product multiplies observables after it sorts them by the causal order of their spacetime supports.
definition: In perturbative quantum field theory, the time-ordered product is a symmetric multilinear map $T$ that sends [observables](c:observable) $A_1,\dots,A_n$ to an observable $T(A_1\cdots A_n)$ in the [Wick algebra](c:wick-algebra), with $T(A)=A$. It obeys causal factorization: if the spacetime supports of $A_1,\dots,A_k$ all lie later in time than those of $A_{k+1},\dots,A_n$, then $T(A_1\cdots A_n)=T(A_1\cdots A_k)\cdot T(A_{k+1}\cdots A_n)$.
examples: For the free scalar field, $T(\phi(x)\phi(y))=\phi(x)\phi(y)$ if $x^0>y^0$ and $T(\phi(x)\phi(y))=\phi(y)\phi(x)$ if $y^0>x^0$.
For observables with spacelike separated supports, neither precedes the other, and the factors commute, so the time-ordered product is their ordinary product.
Non-example: the plain operator product $\phi(x)\phi(y)$ is not the time-ordered product, because for timelike separated points it depends on the order of the factors.

reminder: A time-reversible process has the same joint distributions when time runs backwards.
definition: A [stationary stochastic process](c:stationary-stochastic-process) $(X_t)$ is time-reversible when, for all times $t_1,\dots,t_k$ and every shift $s$, the [joint distribution](c:joint-distribution) of $(X_{t_1},\dots,X_{t_k})$ equals that of $(X_{s-t_1},\dots,X_{s-t_k})$. In words, the process and its [time reversal](c:time-reversal) have the same law.
examples: A real stationary Gaussian process is time-reversible, because its covariance $r(t)$ is an even function of $t$.
A stationary Markov chain whose transition probabilities satisfy [detailed balance](c:detailed-balance) with respect to its stationary distribution is time-reversible.
Non-example: the stationary Markov chain on $\{0,1,2\}$ that moves $0\to1\to2\to0$ with probability $1$ is not time-reversible, because its reversal moves $0\to2\to1\to0$.

steps: Start with a time-reversible process $(X_t)$; by definition it is a [stationary stochastic process](c:stationary-stochastic-process).
Stationarity says that all joint distributions are unchanged when time shifts.
Time-reversibility adds that they are also unchanged when time is flipped by $t\mapsto -t$.
So a time-reversible process is a stationary process with a flip symmetry.
links.why: It shows that reversibility is stationarity plus one more symmetry, so every stationary result applies.

reminder: A timelike curve in a Lorentzian spacetime has a tangent vector with negative squared length at every point.
definition: Let $(X,g)$ be a [Lorentzian manifold](c:lorentzian-manifold) with signature $(-,+,\dots,+)$. A [tangent vector](c:tangent-space) $v\in T_xX$ is timelike when $g(v,v)<0$, and a [curve](c:curve) $\gamma$ in $X$ is timelike when its tangent vector $\dot\gamma(t)$ is timelike for every $t$.
examples: In Minkowski space with $g=-dt^2+dx^2+dy^2+dz^2$, the curve $t\mapsto(t,0,0,0)$ is timelike.
The curve $t\mapsto(t,vt,0,0)$ with $|v|<1$ is timelike, because $g(\dot\gamma,\dot\gamma)=-1+v^2<0$.
Non-example: the light ray $t\mapsto(t,t,0,0)$ is not timelike, because $g(\dot\gamma,\dot\gamma)=-1+1=0$, so it is null.

steps: Take a smooth [curve](c:curve) $\gamma:I\to X$ in a Lorentzian manifold.
At each parameter $t$ the tangent vector $\dot\gamma(t)$ lies in the tangent space at $\gamma(t)$.
Add the condition $g(\dot\gamma(t),\dot\gamma(t))<0$ for all $t$.
Then $\gamma$ is a timelike curve.
links.why: It shows that a timelike curve is a curve with one sign condition on its speed, so curve results still apply.

reminder: The Toeplitz determinant $D_n(f)$ is the determinant of the $n\times n$ matrix with entries $\hat f_{j-k}$.
definition: For an integrable function $f$ on the unit circle with Fourier coefficients $\hat f_m=\frac1{2\pi}\int_0^{2\pi}f(e^{i\theta})e^{-im\theta}\,d\theta$, the Toeplitz determinant is $D_n(f)=\det(\hat f_{j-k})_{j,k=0}^{n-1}$. It is the [determinant](c:determinant) of the $n\times n$ [Toeplitz matrix](c:toeplitz-matrix) with symbol $f$, built from the [Fourier](c:fourier-series) coefficients of $f$.
examples: For $f=1$ the matrix is the identity, and $D_n(f)=1$.
For $f(e^{i\theta})=2-2\cos\theta$ the matrix has $2$ on the diagonal and $-1$ next to it, and $D_n(f)=n+1$.
Non-example: the Hankel determinant $\det(\hat f_{j+k})$ is not a Toeplitz determinant, because its entries depend on $j+k$, not on $j-k$.

steps: Take an $n\times n$ [matrix](c:matrix) $M$ and its [determinant](c:determinant) $\det M$.
Choose $M=(\hat f_{j-k})$, the Toeplitz matrix of a function $f$.
Then the determinant of $M$ equals $D_n(f)$ by definition.
So $D_n(f)$ is the determinant restricted to Toeplitz matrices.
links.why: It shows that all determinant tools apply, while the Toeplitz structure gives extra tools such as asymptotics in $n$.

reminder: A Toeplitz matrix has constant entries along each diagonal, so the entry $t_{jk}$ depends only on $j-k$.
definition: A [matrix](c:matrix) $T=(t_{jk})$ is a Toeplitz matrix when $t_{jk}=c_{j-k}$ for some numbers $c_m$, that is, when each diagonal of $T$ is constant. An $n\times n$ Toeplitz matrix is fixed by its $2n-1$ numbers $c_{-(n-1)},\dots,c_{n-1}$.
examples: The matrix with $2$ on the diagonal and $-1$ on the two neighboring diagonals is Toeplitz.
The identity matrix and the matrix of all ones are Toeplitz.
Non-example: the Hilbert matrix with entries $1/(j+k+1)$ is not Toeplitz, because its entries are constant along anti-diagonals, not along diagonals.

steps: Take any $n\times n$ [matrix](c:matrix) $T=(t_{jk})$.
Impose $t_{jk}=t_{j+1,k+1}$ for all valid $j,k$.
This makes every diagonal of $T$ constant.
So $T$ is a Toeplitz matrix.
links.why: It shows that a Toeplitz matrix is a matrix with a shift symmetry, which leaves only $2n-1$ free numbers.

reminder: A torsion module is a module in which every element is killed by some nonzero ring element.
definition: Let $R$ be an [integral domain](c:integral-domain). An element $m$ of an $R$-[module](c:module) $M$ is a torsion element when $rm=0$ for some nonzero $r\in R$, and $M$ is a torsion module when all its elements are torsion elements.
examples: Every finite abelian group is a torsion $\mathbb{Z}$-module, because $|G|\cdot g=0$ for every $g\in G$.
The group $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$ is a torsion $\mathbb{Z}$-module: the element $m/n$ is killed by $n$.
Non-example: $\mathbb{Z}$ as a $\mathbb{Z}$-module is not torsion, because $r\cdot1=0$ forces $r=0$; and $\mathbb{Z}\oplus\mathbb{Z}/2$ is not torsion, because $(1,0)$ is not a torsion element.

steps: Take an $R$-[module](c:module) $M$ over an integral domain $R$.
Add the condition that for each $m\in M$ some nonzero $r\in R$ gives $rm=0$.
Then $M$ is a torsion module.
links.why: It shows that a torsion module is a module with one extra condition, the opposite of being torsion-free.

steps: Let $G$ be a [finite abelian group](c:finite-abelian-group); it is a $\mathbb{Z}$-module.
Each $g\in G$ satisfies $|G|\,g=0$, and $|G|\ne0$.
So $G$ is a torsion module over $\mathbb{Z}$.
links.why: It shows that torsion modules extend finite abelian groups to other rings and to infinite groups such as $\mathbb{Q}/\mathbb{Z}$.

reminder:
The torsion tensor of a connection $
abla$ is $T(X,Y)=
abla_XY-
abla_YX-[X,Y]$.
definition:
Let $
abla$ be an [affine connection](c:affine-connection) on a manifold. Its torsion tensor is the map $T(X,Y)=
abla_XY-
abla_YX-[X,Y]$ on [vector fields](c:vector-field) $X,Y$, where $[X,Y]$ is the [Lie bracket](c:lie-bracket). It is $C^\infty$-bilinear and antisymmetric in $X$ and $Y$, so it is a tensor of type $(1,2)$, and the connection is torsion-free when $T=0$.
examples: On $\mathbb{R}^n$ the flat connection $\nabla_XY=X(Y^i)\partial_i$ has $T=0$.
On a [Lie group](c:lie-group) $G$, the connection with $\nabla_XY=0$ for left-invariant fields $X,Y$ has $T(X,Y)=-[X,Y]$.
Non-example: the expression $\nabla_XY-\nabla_YX$ alone is not a tensor, because replacing $Y$ by $fY$ adds the term $X(f)Y$, so it is not $C^\infty$-linear in $Y$.

reminder: The total complex of a double complex has, in degree $k$, the direct sum of all terms $C_{p,q}$ with $p+q=k$.
definition: Let $C_{\bullet,\bullet}$ be a [double complex](c:double-complex) with commuting horizontal and vertical differentials $d^h$ and $d^v$. Its total complex is the [chain complex](c:chain-complex) whose degree $k$ term is the [direct sum](c:direct-sum) $\mathrm{Tot}(C)_k=\bigoplus_{p+q=k}C_{p,q}$, with [differential](c:differential) $d=d^h+(-1)^pd^v$ on $C_{p,q}$; the sign makes $d^2=0$.
examples: For chain complexes $A$ and $B$, the double complex $C_{p,q}=A_p\otimes B_q$ has the tensor product complex $A\otimes B$ as total complex.
If a double complex has only one nonzero row $q=0$, then $\mathrm{Tot}(C)_k=C_{k,0}$, which is the row itself.
Non-example: the product $\prod_{p+q=k}C_{p,q}$ is not the total complex defined here, because it is the product totalization, which differs when infinitely many terms have total degree $k$.

reminder: The total curvature of a curve is the integral of its curvature with respect to arc length.
definition: For a smooth [curve](c:curve) $\gamma$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$ parametrized by arc length $s\in[0,L]$, the total curvature is the [integral](c:integral) $\int_0^L\kappa(s)\,ds$, where $\kappa=\lVert\gamma''\rVert$ is the [curvature](c:curvature). It equals the length of the path that the unit tangent vector traces on the unit sphere.
examples: A circle of radius $r$ has curvature $1/r$ and length $2\pi r$, so its total curvature is $2\pi$ for every $r$.
A straight line has total curvature $0$.
Non-example: the integral $\int K\,dA$ of the [Gaussian curvature](c:gaussian-curvature) of a surface is a different quantity, because it integrates over area, not along a curve.

reminder: The total derivative of $t\mapsto f(g_1(t),\dots,g_n(t))$ is the sum of $\partial_if\cdot g_i'(t)$ over all variables.
definition: Let $f$ be a differentiable [function](c:function) of $n$ variables and $g_1,\dots,g_n$ differentiable functions of $t$. The total [derivative](c:derivative) of $t\mapsto f(g_1(t),\dots,g_n(t))$ is $\sum_{i=1}^n\frac{\partial f}{\partial x_i}(g(t))\,g_i'(t)$, a [linear combination](c:linear-combination) of the [partial derivatives](c:partial-derivative). More generally, the total derivative of a differentiable map $f$ at $a$ is the linear map $Df(a)$ with $f(a+h)=f(a)+Df(a)h+o(\lVert h\rVert)$.
examples: For $f(x,y)=xy$ and $g(t)=(\cos t,\sin t)$, the total derivative is $\sin t\cdot(-\sin t)+\cos t\cdot\cos t=\cos 2t$.
For $f(x,t)=x^2t$ and $x=\sin t$, the total derivative is $2xt\cos t+x^2$, which includes the direct dependence on $t$.
Non-example: the partial derivative $\partial f/\partial x_1$ is not the total derivative, because it holds the other variables fixed while the $g_i$ change with $t$.

steps: Let $g_1(t)=a_1+t$ and let $g_i(t)=a_i$ be constant for $i>1$.
Then $g_1'(t)=1$ and $g_i'(t)=0$ for $i>1$.
The sum then reduces to the single term $\partial f/\partial x_1$ at the point $(a_1+t,a_2,\dots,a_n)$.
So the [partial derivative](c:partial-derivative) is the total derivative along a line parallel to the first axis.
links.why: It shows that a partial derivative is the special case where only one variable moves.

reminder: The total variation distance of two probability measures is the largest difference of the probabilities that they give to one event.
definition: For [probability measures](c:probability-measure) $P$ and $Q$ on a space with a [sigma-algebra](c:sigma-algebra) $\mathcal F$, the total variation distance is $d_{TV}(P,Q)=\sup_{A\in\mathcal F}|P(A)-Q(A)|$, where the [supremum](c:least-upper-bound) runs over all events. For discrete distributions with mass functions $p$ and $q$, it equals $\tfrac12\sum_x|p(x)-q(x)|$.
examples: For Bernoulli distributions with parameters $p$ and $q$, the distance is $|p-q|$.
Two point masses $\delta_a$ and $\delta_b$ with $a\ne b$ have distance $1$.
Non-example: the Kullback-Leibler divergence is not a total variation distance, because it is not symmetric and it can be larger than $1$.

reminder: A submanifold of a Riemannian manifold is totally geodesic when each of its geodesics is also a geodesic of the ambient manifold.
definition: Let $\Sigma$ be a [submanifold](c:submanifold) of a [Riemannian manifold](c:riemannian-manifold) $X$, with the induced metric. Then $\Sigma$ is totally geodesic when every [geodesic](c:geodesic) of $\Sigma$ is a geodesic of $X$; equivalently, its [second fundamental form](c:second-fundamental-form) vanishes.
examples: Every great circle of the sphere $S^2$ is a totally geodesic curve, and every great $k$-sphere is totally geodesic in $S^n$.
Every straight line and every affine subspace is totally geodesic in $\mathbb{R}^n$.
Non-example: a latitude circle other than the equator is not totally geodesic in $S^2$, because it is not a great circle, so it is not a geodesic of $S^2$.

steps: Let $\Sigma\subset X$ be a [submanifold](c:submanifold) of a Riemannian manifold, with the induced metric.
Add the condition that each geodesic of $\Sigma$ is also a geodesic of $X$.
Equivalently, the second fundamental form of $\Sigma$ in $X$ vanishes.
Then $\Sigma$ is totally geodesic.
links.why: It shows that totally geodesic is a curvature condition on how the submanifold sits in the ambient space.

reminder: A trace-class operator is a compact operator on a Hilbert space whose singular values have a finite sum.
definition: A [compact operator](c:compact-operator) $T$ on a [Hilbert space](c:hilbert-space) $H$ is trace class when its singular values $s_1\ge s_2\ge\dots$ satisfy $\sum_ns_n<\infty$. Then the [trace](c:trace-of-a-matrix) $\operatorname{tr}T=\sum_n\langle Te_n,e_n\rangle$ converges absolutely for every orthonormal basis $(e_n)$ and does not depend on the basis.
examples: Every finite-rank operator is trace class, and its trace is the trace of its matrix.
The diagonal operator with entries $1/n^2$ is trace class, with trace $\pi^2/6$.
Non-example: the diagonal operator with entries $1/n$ is compact but not trace class, because $\sum1/n$ diverges.

steps: Let $T$ be trace class, so its singular values $s_n$ satisfy $\sum s_n<\infty$.
The terms of a convergent series tend to zero, so $s_n\to0$.
An operator on a Hilbert space whose singular values tend to $0$ is a norm limit of finite-rank operators.
So $T$ is a [compact operator](c:compact-operator); the trace-class case adds that the singular values are summable.
links.why: It shows that trace-class operators have all properties of compact operators, plus a well-defined trace.

reminder: If a property passes from all smaller elements to each element of a well-ordered set, it holds for every element.
definition: Let $(W,<)$ be a [well-ordered set](c:is-well-order), for example the [ordinals](c:ordinal), and let $P$ be a property of its elements. Transfinite induction says: if for every $\alpha\in W$ the statement '$P(\beta)$ for all $\beta<\alpha$' implies $P(\alpha)$, then $P(\alpha)$ holds for every $\alpha\in W$.
examples: A strictly increasing map $f$ from the ordinals to the ordinals satisfies $f(\beta)\ge\beta$ for all $\beta$, by transfinite induction on $\beta$.
Ordinary induction on $\mathbb{N}$ is the case $W=\mathbb{N}$, where the step for $\alpha=0$ has an empty hypothesis.

Non-example: $\mathbb{Z}$ is not well-ordered, and induction fails on it: for the false property $P$, the premise '$P(m)$ for all $m<n$' is false for every $n$, so each step holds, yet $P$ holds nowhere.

steps: Let $(W,<)$ be a well-ordered set.
A well-order has no infinite descending chain, so the relation $<$ is well-founded.
[Well-founded induction](c:well-founded-induction) therefore applies to $W$ and gives the same principle.
So transfinite induction is well-founded induction on a well-order.
links.why: It shows that transfinite induction needs only that no infinite descending chain exists, which also covers trees and other orders.

reminder: Transgression turns an $n$-form on $X$ into an $(n-k)$-form on the mapping space $[\Sigma,X]$ by integrating over a closed $k$-manifold $\Sigma$.
definition: Let $\omega$ be a [differential form](c:differential-form) of degree $n$ on a smooth space $X$, and let $\Sigma$ be an oriented [closed manifold](c:closed-manifold) of dimension $k\le n$. With the [evaluation map](c:evaluation-map) $\mathrm{ev}:\Sigma\times[\Sigma,X]\to X$, the transgression is $\tau_\Sigma\omega=\int_\Sigma\mathrm{ev}^*\omega$, the [integration](c:integration-of-differential-forms) of the pullback along $\Sigma$; it is a differential form of degree $n-k$ on the mapping space $[\Sigma,X]$.
examples: For $\Sigma=S^1$ and a $2$-form $\omega$ on $X$, the transgression is a $1$-form on the free loop space, $(\tau\omega)_\gamma(v)=\int_{S^1}\omega(\dot\gamma,v)\,dt$.
For $k=n$ the transgression is a function: $\tau_\Sigma\omega(f)=\int_\Sigma f^*\omega$ for each map $f:\Sigma\to X$.

Non-example: $\mathrm{ev}^*\omega$ alone is not a transgression, because it lives on $\Sigma\times[\Sigma,X]$ and has degree $n$; only integration over $\Sigma$ gives a form of degree $n-k$ on $[\Sigma,X]$.

reminder: A transversal gate acts on an error-correcting code as a tensor product of gates that each touch one physical subsystem.
definition: Let an [error-correcting code](c:error-correcting-code) be a subspace of $H_1\otimes\cdots\otimes H_n$, with $n$ physical subsystems. A logical gate is transversal when it is implemented by a [tensor product](c:tensor-product) $U_1\otimes\cdots\otimes U_n$ of [unitary operators](c:unitary-operator), each acting on one subsystem, that maps the code space to itself. For gates on several code blocks, each $U_i$ acts on the $i$-th subsystems of all blocks, so one faulty component spreads no error inside a block.
examples: On the three-qubit [bit flip code](c:bit-flip-code), the product $X\otimes X\otimes X$ is a transversal logical $X$ gate.
On the seven-qubit Steane code, applying the Hadamard gate to each of the seven qubits gives a logical Hadamard gate.
Non-example: on the bit flip code, $H\otimes H\otimes H$ is not a logical gate, because it sends $|000\rangle$ to $|{+}{+}{+}\rangle$, which lies outside the code space.

reminder: A tree automaton reads a tree from the leaves to the root, one state per node, and accepts if the root state is final.
definition: A bottom-up tree automaton over a ranked alphabet $\Sigma$ is a tuple $(Q,\Sigma,\delta,F)$ with a finite set $Q$ of states, a set $F\subseteq Q$ of final states, and for each symbol $f$ of arity $k$ a transition map $\delta_f:Q^k\to Q$. It assigns to each node of a [tree](c:tree) labelled by $\Sigma$ the state computed from the states of its children, and it accepts the tree when the root state lies in $F$.
examples: Over a leaf symbol $a$ and a binary symbol $f$, the automaton with states $\{0,1\}$, $\delta_a=1$ and $\delta_f(p,q)=p+q \bmod 2$ accepts the trees with an even number of leaves, for $F=\{0\}$.
An automaton can evaluate Boolean expression trees with leaves $0,1$ and inner nodes $\wedge,\vee$, and accept those with value $1$.

Non-example: the set of trees $f(s,t)$ in which $s$ and $t$ have equally many $a$-leaves is not recognized by any tree automaton, because finitely many states cannot count the $a$-leaves without bound.

steps: Take a [finite automaton](c:finite-automaton) over an alphabet $A$ with transition function $\delta:Q\times A\to Q$.
Write a word $a_1\dots a_n$ as the tree $a_n(\dots a_1(\#)\dots)$ built from unary symbols $a\in A$ and one leaf $\#$.
Let the tree automaton start in the initial state at $\#$ and apply $\delta_a(q)=\delta(q,a)$ on the way up.
It reaches the root in the state that the word automaton has after reading the word, so both accept the same words.
links.why: It shows that tree automata include word automata as the case of unary trees, so results for words are special cases.

reminder: An upper triangular matrix has only zeros below its diagonal, and a lower triangular matrix has only zeros above it.
definition: A square [matrix](c:matrix) $A=(a_{ij})$ is upper triangular when $a_{ij}=0$ for all $i>j$, and lower triangular when $a_{ij}=0$ for all $i<j$. A triangular matrix is one of these two kinds, and its [determinant](c:determinant) is the product of its diagonal entries.
examples: The matrix $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\0&3\end{pmatrix}$ is upper triangular, and its determinant is $1\cdot3=3$.
Every diagonal matrix is both upper triangular and lower triangular.
Non-example: $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\3&4\end{pmatrix}$ is not triangular, because it has nonzero entries both above and below the diagonal.

steps: Let $D=(d_{ij})$ be a [diagonal matrix](c:diagonal-matrix), so $d_{ij}=0$ whenever $i\ne j$.
Then $d_{ij}=0$ for all $i>j$, so $D$ is upper triangular.
Likewise $d_{ij}=0$ for all $i<j$, so $D$ is lower triangular.
A triangular matrix may have nonzero entries on one side of the diagonal.
links.why: It shows that triangular matrices include the diagonal ones, so triangular results cover diagonal matrices.

reminder: A tubular neighbourhood of a submanifold is an open neighbourhood that looks like its normal bundle.
definition: Let $X\subseteq Y$ be a submanifold, given by an [embedding](c:embedding-of-differentiable-manifolds) of [manifolds](c:manifold). A tubular neighbourhood of $X$ in $Y$ is an [open neighbourhood](c:open-neighbourhood) $U$ of $X$ together with a diffeomorphism from $U$ onto the total space of the [normal bundle](c:normal-bundle) of $X$, a [vector bundle](c:vector-bundle), that is the identity on $X$ viewed as the zero section.
examples: For the circle $X=S^1\subset\mathbb{R}^2$, the open annulus $\{1/2<|x|<2\}$ is a tubular neighbourhood, and it is diffeomorphic to $S^1\times\mathbb{R}$.
For a point $X=\{p\}$ in $Y$, a chart ball around $p$ is a tubular neighbourhood, with the normal bundle $T_pY$ over one point.
Non-example: the figure eight in $\mathbb{R}^2$ has no tubular neighbourhood, because it is not a submanifold: no neighbourhood of the crossing looks like a line.

reminder: A set $A$ is Turing reducible to $B$ when an oracle machine decides $A$ with the help of answers about membership in $B$.
definition: A set $A\subseteq\mathbb{N}$ is Turing reducible to a set $B\subseteq\mathbb{N}$, written $A\le_TB$, when some [oracle machine](c:oracle-machine) with oracle $B$ decides $A$: on input $n$ it halts and tells whether $n\in A$, after asking finitely many questions of the form 'is $m$ in $B$?'. A set is [computable](c:computable-set) exactly when it is Turing reducible to the empty set, that is, when no oracle is needed.
examples: Every computable set is Turing reducible to every set, because the machine can ignore its oracle.
Every set is Turing reducible to its complement, because the machine asks the oracle about $n$ and flips the answer.
Non-example: the halting set $K$ is not Turing reducible to a computable set, because then a [Turing machine](c:turing-machine) without oracle would decide $K$.

reminder: The turning number of a closed regular plane curve counts how many times its tangent vector turns around.
definition: Let $\gamma:[0,1]\to\mathbb{R}^2$ be a smooth [closed curve](c:closed-curve) with $\gamma'(t)\ne0$ for all $t$, that is, an [immersion](c:immersion) of the circle. Its turning number is the [degree](c:degree-of-a-map) of the map $t\mapsto\gamma'(t)/\lVert\gamma'(t)\rVert$ from the circle to the unit circle: the total change of the tangent angle divided by $2\pi$.
examples: A circle traversed once counterclockwise has turning number $1$, and traversed clockwise it has turning number $-1$.
A figure eight has turning number $0$.
Non-example: a closed curve with cusps, such as the astroid, has no turning number as defined here, because its tangent vector vanishes at the cusps.

steps: Let $\gamma$ be a regular closed curve in the plane.
Its unit tangent gives a continuous map $T:S^1\to S^1$.
The [degree](c:degree-of-a-map) of a map $S^1\to S^1$ counts how many times it winds around the circle.
The turning number of $\gamma$ is the degree of $T$.
links.why: It shows that the turning number is a degree, so homotopy invariance of degree makes it constant under regular homotopy.

reminder: A twin prime is a prime number $p$ such that $p+2$ or $p-2$ is also prime.
definition: A twin prime is a [prime number](c:prime-number) $p$ for which $p-2$ or $p+2$ is also prime. A pair $(p,p+2)$ in which both entries are prime is a twin prime pair.
examples: The number $5$ belongs to two twin prime pairs, $(3,5)$ and $(5,7)$.
Non-example: $23$ is prime, but $21=3\cdot7$ and $25=5^2$ are not, so $23$ is not a twin prime.

steps: Let $p$ be a [prime number](c:prime-number).
Add the condition that $p+2$ is prime or $p-2$ is prime.
Then $p$ is a twin prime.
links.why: It shows that twin primes are the primes at distance $2$ from another prime, so every result on primes applies to them.

reminder: A twisting cochain is a degree $1$ map from a dg-coalgebra to a dg-algebra that solves the Maurer-Cartan equation.
definition: Let $(C,d_C,\Delta)$ be a dg-[coalgebra](c:coalgebra) and $(A,d_A,\mu)$ a [dg-algebra](c:dg-algebra-2). A twisting cochain is a linear map $\tau:C\to A$ of degree $1$ with $d_A\tau+\tau d_C+\mu(\tau\otimes\tau)\Delta=0$, up to the sign convention. This says that $\tau$ solves the [Maurer-Cartan equation](c:maurer-cartan-equation) in the [convolution algebra](c:convolution-algebra) $\mathrm{Hom}(C,A)$.
examples: The zero map $\tau=0$ is a twisting cochain.
For a dg-coalgebra $C$, the canonical map $C\to\Omega C$ into its cobar construction is a twisting cochain.
Non-example: if $\tau$ is a twisting cochain with $\mu(\tau\otimes\tau)\Delta\ne0$, then $2\tau$ is not one, because the quadratic term scales by $4$ while the linear terms scale by $2$.

steps: Form the graded space $\mathrm{Hom}(C,A)$ with the convolution product $f\star g=\mu(f\otimes g)\Delta$.
Give it the differential $\partial f=d_Af-(-1)^{|f|}fd_C$, so that it becomes a dg-algebra.
An element $\tau$ of degree $1$ solves the [Maurer-Cartan equation](c:maurer-cartan-equation) when $\partial\tau+\tau\star\tau=0$.
That equation is the twisting cochain condition.
links.why: It shows that twisting cochains are Maurer-Cartan elements of one convolution dg-algebra, so Maurer-Cartan theory applies.

reminder: An $\varepsilon$-typical sequence of a source has probability close to $2^{-nH}$, where $H$ is the entropy.
definition: Let $X_1,\dots,X_n$ be [independent identically distributed](c:iid-random-variables) draws from a [probability distribution](c:probability-distribution) $p$ with [entropy](c:entropy) $H$. A sequence $x^n=(x_1,\dots,x_n)$ is $\varepsilon$-typical when $2^{-n(H+\varepsilon)}\le p(x^n)\le2^{-n(H-\varepsilon)}$, where $p(x^n)=\prod_ip(x_i)$.
examples: For a fair coin, $H=1$ and $p(x^n)=2^{-n}$, so every sequence of length $n$ is $\varepsilon$-typical.
For a coin with $P(1)=0.1$, a sequence with about $n/10$ ones is typical, because then $-\tfrac1n\log_2p(x^n)\approx0.469=H$.
Non-example: for the coin with $P(1)=0.1$, the all-zero sequence has $-\tfrac1n\log_2p(x^n)\approx0.152$, which is far from $H\approx0.469$, so it is not typical for small $\varepsilon$.

reminder: The typical set is the set of $\varepsilon$-typical sequences of length $n$; for large $n$ it has probability close to $1$.
definition: For a source with [entropy](c:entropy) $H$, the typical set $A_\varepsilon^{(n)}$ is the set of all $\varepsilon$-typical [sequences](c:typical-sequence) $x^n$ of length $n$, those with $2^{-n(H+\varepsilon)}\le p(x^n)\le2^{-n(H-\varepsilon)}$. For large $n$ it has probability above $1-\varepsilon$, and it has at most $2^{n(H+\varepsilon)}$ elements.
examples: For a fair coin, the typical set is the set of all $2^n$ sequences.
For a coin with $P(1)=0.1$, the typical set holds the sequences with about $10\%$ ones; it has about $2^{0.469n}$ elements, far fewer than $2^n$.
Non-example: for a coin with $P(1)=0.1$, the all-zero sequence is the single most probable sequence, yet it is not in the typical set.

reminder: Uniform approximation means that for every $\varepsilon>0$ some function in the class stays within $\varepsilon$ of $f$ at every point.
definition: Let $E$ be a set and $\mathcal F$ a class of [functions](c:function) on $E$. A function $f$ can be uniformly approximated by $\mathcal F$ on $E$ when for every $\varepsilon>0$ there is $g\in\mathcal F$ with $\sup_{x\in E}|f(x)-g(x)|<\varepsilon$. Equivalently, some sequence in $\mathcal F$ converges to $f$ with [uniform convergence](c:uniform-convergence) on $E$.
examples: By the Weierstrass theorem, every continuous function on $[a,b]$ is uniformly approximated by polynomials.
The Taylor polynomials of $e^x$ approximate $e^x$ uniformly on $[0,1]$.

Non-example: polynomials cannot uniformly approximate $1/z$ on the unit circle, because $\oint p\,dz=0$ for every polynomial $p$ while $\oint z^{-1}dz=2\pi i$, so no polynomial stays within distance less than $1$ of $1/z$ on the whole circle.

reminder: A sequence of functions is uniformly bounded when one constant $M$ bounds every function at every point.
definition: A [sequence](c:sequence) $(f_n)$ of real or complex functions on a set $E$ is uniformly bounded when there is one number $M$ with $|f_n(x)|\le M$ for all $n$ and all $x\in E$. Each $f_n$ is then a [bounded function](c:bounded-function), and the bound does not depend on $n$.
examples: The functions $f_n(x)=\sin(nx)$ on $\mathbb{R}$ satisfy $|f_n|\le1$, so they are uniformly bounded.
The functions $f_n(x)=x^n$ on $[0,1]$ are uniformly bounded by $1$.
Non-example: $f_n(x)=nx$ on $[0,1]$ is a [sequence](c:sequence) of bounded functions, but $\sup|f_n|=n$ grows without bound, so it is not uniformly bounded.

steps: Let $f$ be a [bounded function](c:bounded-function) on $E$ with $|f|\le M$.
Take the constant sequence $f_n=f$.
Then $|f_n(x)|\le M$ for all $n$ and all $x$.
So a single bounded function gives a uniformly bounded sequence.
links.why: It shows that uniform boundedness is boundedness with one bound shared by the whole sequence.

reminder: A unimodal function rises to one peak and then falls, so every set $\{f\ge c\}$ is an interval.
definition: A real function $f$ on an [interval](c:interval) is unimodal when there is a point $m$ such that $f$ is [monotone](c:monotone-function) on each side of $m$: non-decreasing to the left and non-increasing to the right. Equivalently, every superlevel set $\{x:f(x)\ge c\}$ is a [convex set](c:convex-set), that is, an interval; on $\mathbb{R}^n$ this second form is the definition.
examples: The standard normal density $e^{-x^2/2}/\sqrt{2\pi}$ is unimodal with mode $0$.
A [concave function](c:concave-function) such as $1-x^2$ on $[-1,1]$ is unimodal.

Non-example: the mixture density $\tfrac12\varphi(x-3)+\tfrac12\varphi(x+3)$, with $\varphi$ the standard normal density, is not unimodal, because $\{f\ge c\}$ is two separate intervals for $c$ slightly below the peak.

steps: Let $f$ be a [concave function](c:concave-function) on an interval.
For every $c$ the set $\{f\ge c\}$ is convex, because $f(\lambda x+(1-\lambda)y)\ge\min(f(x),f(y))\ge c$.
A function whose superlevel sets are all intervals is unimodal.
So every concave function is unimodal, but not conversely, as the bell-shaped normal density shows.
links.why: It shows that unimodality is a weaker shape condition than concavity, so results for unimodal functions cover concave ones.

reminder: A unipotent flow is the action of a one-parameter unipotent subgroup of $G$ on a homogeneous space $G/\Gamma$.
definition: Let $G$ be a [Lie group](c:lie-group) and $\Gamma$ a [lattice](c:lattice-discrete-subgroup) in $G$. A one-parameter subgroup $u_t=\exp(tN)$ of $G$ is unipotent when $\mathrm{Ad}(u_t)$ is a unipotent linear map, that is, when $\mathrm{ad}\,N$ is nilpotent. The unipotent flow is the [flow](c:flow) $\varphi_t(g\Gamma)=u_tg\Gamma$ on $G/\Gamma$.
examples: On $SL_2(\mathbb{R})/SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$, the horocycle flow with $u_t=\begin{pmatrix}1&t\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ is a unipotent flow.
On the torus $\mathbb{R}^n/\mathbb{Z}^n$, every linear flow $x\mapsto x+tv$ is a unipotent flow, because $G=\mathbb{R}^n$ is abelian and $\mathrm{Ad}$ is trivial.

Non-example: the geodesic flow on $SL_2(\mathbb{R})/SL_2(\mathbb{Z})$, given by $a_t=\mathrm{diag}(e^{t/2},e^{-t/2})$, is not unipotent, because $\mathrm{Ad}(a_t)$ has the eigenvalues $e^{t}$ and $e^{-t}$.

steps: Let $\mathbb{R}$ act on $G/\Gamma$ by $t\cdot g\Gamma=u_tg\Gamma$.
This is a [flow](c:flow), because $u_0=e$ and $u_{s+t}=u_su_t$.
Add the condition that $\mathrm{Ad}(u_t)$ is unipotent.
Then the flow is a unipotent flow.
links.why: It shows that a unipotent flow is a flow of a special algebraic kind, which is what Ratner's theorems use.

reminder: An integral domain has unique factorization when every nonzero non-unit is a product of irreducible elements in one way, up to order and units.
definition: An [integral domain](c:integral-domain) $R$ has unique factorization when every nonzero non-unit of $R$ is a product of [irreducible elements](c:irreducible), and any two such products have the same number of factors that match up to order and multiplication by [units](c:group-of-units). A ring with this property is a unique factorization domain.
examples: The integers $\mathbb{Z}$ have unique factorization: $12=2\cdot2\cdot3$, up to order and signs.
The polynomial ring $k[x]$ over a field $k$ has unique factorization.
Non-example: in $\mathbb{Z}[\sqrt{-5}]$ we have $6=2\cdot3=(1+\sqrt{-5})(1-\sqrt{-5})$, two factorizations into irreducibles that do not match.

steps: Let $R$ be a [principal ideal domain](c:principal-ideal-domain).
Every nonzero non-unit of $R$ is a product of irreducibles, because ascending chains of ideals stop.
Every irreducible element of $R$ is prime, because the ideal it generates is maximal.
Prime factors give uniqueness up to order and units, so $R$ has unique factorization.
links.why: It shows that unique factorization holds in every principal ideal domain, such as $\mathbb{Z}$ and $k[x]$.

steps: Start with an [integral domain](c:integral-domain) $R$.
Add the condition that every nonzero non-unit is a product of irreducible elements.
Add the condition that two such products agree up to order and units.
Then $R$ has unique factorization.
links.why: It shows which two conditions make an integral domain a unique factorization domain.
